questions.question: What is @WebMvcTest and what does it load?
questions.title: @WebMvcTest Purpose
questions.direct_answer: @WebMvcTest is a Spring Boot MVC test slice. It limits scanning to controllers and other supported MVC-related types, applies MVC-focused auto-configuration, and auto-configures MockMvc without opening a server port. Ordinary service and repository beans are not discovered, but filters, controller advice, converters, security configuration types, imports, and test bean overrides can all be part of the context.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands slice testing and can isolate the web layer for focused controller tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every test, loading the entire application context and making tests slow
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that missing controller collaborators can be supplied with current @MockitoBean, older Boot @MockBean, @Import, or a small test configuration, depending on whether the collaborator should be mocked or real

sections.title: What @WebMvcTest Does for You
sections.content:
@WebMvcTest is a Spring Boot **MVC test slice**. It limits component scanning to supported MVC-related types and applies auto-configuration for controller testing, including MockMvc. Depending on the application and classpath, the slice can include controllers, controller advice, JSON components, converters, filters, and security-related configuration types.

Ordinary @Service and @Repository beans are not discovered by the slice. Supply a missing controller collaborator with current **@MockitoBean**, with **@MockBean** on older Boot versions, or import a small real configuration when its behavior belongs in the test. Startup time and bean count depend on configuration, and a failure can come from mapping, validation, serialization, filters, advice, security, or test setup—not only controller code.

sections.title: @WebMvcTest at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|@WebMvcTest|~MVC slice|controller selection|MVC auto-configuration|MockMvc, no server port
emerald|Supported web types|~May be included|controller advice|converters and filters|security configuration types
rose|Not discovered normally|~Outside MVC slice|service beans|repository beans|database infrastructure
amber|Provide a collaborator|~Choose intent|@MockitoBean current|@MockBean older Boot|@Import for a real component

sections.title: Testing a Controller with @WebMvcTest
When to Use @WebMvcTest
sections.content:
Use **@WebMvcTest** when the behavior belongs to the MVC boundary: request mapping, parameter binding, validation, serialization, HTTP status, controller advice, filters, or security. For example, it can verify that `POST /api/users` rejects invalid JSON or that a query parameter reaches the controller in the expected form.

It does not by itself prove a repository query, transaction, listening server, or remote integration. Use a JPA slice, a broader Boot test, a container-backed component test, or an end-to-end test when that additional boundary is part of the requirement.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Leaving a required collaborator absent**: Supply it as @MockitoBean, older @MockBean, or imported real configuration according to the test boundary.
- **Assuming fixed performance**: The slice usually loads less than a broad context, but imports, filters, security, and custom configuration still affect startup.
- **Assuming every mock must be stubbed**: Stub only calls whose default Mockito result does not express the scenario. The failure from an unstubbed call depends on the controller behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Test slice**: @WebMvcTest limits discovery and auto-configuration to supported MVC concerns rather than loading one fixed list of beans
**MockMvc auto-configured**: You get @Autowired MockMvc for free to simulate HTTP requests without starting a real server
**Missing collaborators**: Provide them with current @MockitoBean, older Boot @MockBean, @Import, or test configuration as appropriate
**Focused startup**: The slice avoids unrelated application layers, but there is no universal startup time
**Security can participate**: With Spring Security on the classpath, security auto-configuration and filters may affect requests; use the test support that matches the security scenario

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @WebMvcTest is Spring Boot's focused MVC slice. It selects a controller-oriented context, applies MVC test auto-configuration, and gives me MockMvc without starting a real server. Ordinary service and repository beans are not discovered, so I provide a required collaborator with @MockitoBean in current Spring, @MockBean on older Boot, or @Import when I intentionally want a small real component. I use the slice for request mappings, validation, serialization, controller advice, filters, and security behavior at the MVC boundary. It normally has less setup than @SpringBootTest, but the time is configuration-dependent and a failing test is not automatically proof of a controller-code bug.

questions.question: How do you write a basic @WebMvcTest to verify a GET endpoint returns 200 OK?
questions.title: Basic @WebMvcTest GET Request
questions.direct_answer: With `@WebMvcTest(MyController.class)`, inject MockMvc, provide any missing controller collaborator with the current `@MockitoBean` support (or `@MockBean` on older Spring Boot versions), stub it only when the response depends on it, then assert the real path: `mockMvc.perform(get("/api/orders/1")).andExpect(status().isOk()).andExpect(jsonPath("$.id").value(1));`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Hands-on ability to write a real controller test using MockMvc—this is the number one practical coding question in fresher interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Calling the wrong route, omitting a required collaborator, or asserting only 200 without checking the response contract
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Walk through the test structure methodically: arrange (stub the mock), act (perform the request), assert (check status and body)

sections.title: Writing Your First MockMvc Test
sections.content:
A basic MockMvc GET test uses **arrange, act, assert**. Arrange any collaborator result the controller needs. Act with `mockMvc.perform(get(...))`. Assert the status and the meaningful response fields. MockMvc runs Spring MVC request handling without opening a network port.

If the controller depends on a bean outside the slice, provide it with current **@MockitoBean**, older Boot **@MockBean**, or a small imported configuration. Stub a Mockito method only when its default result does not match the scenario; an unstubbed call does not universally produce a NullPointerException.

sections.title: How a GET Flows Through MockMvc
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[MockMvc.perform
GET /api/orders/1] --> B[DispatcherServlet] B --> C[OrderController] C --> D[@MockBean OrderService
stubbed result] D --> C C --> E[JSON response] E --> F[andExpect
status + jsonPath] ```

sections.title: Complete GET Endpoint Test
When to Write This Test
sections.content:
Use a MockMvc GET test to check the MVC contract: the real route, parameters, status, headers, content type, and stable response fields. Cover both a successful response and meaningful failures such as invalid input, unauthenticated access, or a missing single resource when the API defines 404.

This test gives evidence about the configured MVC slice, not a guarantee about a repository, remote system, or full deployment. Test service rules separately when direct construction is enough, and add broader integration coverage when the result depends on real Spring, persistence, or infrastructure behavior.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using a different route from the controller mapping**: Assert the actual public path, including path variables and query parameters.
- **Forgetting a needed stub**: Mockito returns type-dependent defaults; the resulting response depends on the controller, so arrange the specific result the scenario requires.
- **Asserting only the status**: Also verify stable contract fields, content type, headers, or error body that matter to the client.
- **Wrong JSONPath**: `$` represents the JSON document root; arrays use paths such as `$[0].name`.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Arrange-Act-Assert pattern**: First stub the mock service (arrange), then perform the HTTP request (act), finally verify status and JSON (assert)
**MockMvc injection**: Use @Autowired MockMvc—it's auto-configured by @WebMvcTest, no manual setup needed
**Scenario-driven stubbing**: Stub the collaborator calls whose results are needed for this response
**Fluent API**: mockMvc.perform(get(path)).andExpect(matcher) reads like English and chains multiple assertions
**jsonPath validation**: Use jsonPath to check JSON response fields without deserializing—jsonPath("$.id").value(1) verifies the id field

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I select the controller with @WebMvcTest, inject MockMvc, and provide any collaborator outside the slice with @MockitoBean, or @MockBean on older Boot. I arrange the exact result needed for the case, call the real public route with mockMvc.perform(get(...)), and assert `status().isOk()` plus the response contract—for example the content type and `jsonPath("$.id")`. Stubbing is scenario-driven: Mockito defaults do not always cause the same failure, so the test should state the collaborator behavior it needs.

questions.question: What does @WebMvcTest NOT load and what do you have to provide yourself?
questions.title: What @WebMvcTest Excludes
questions.direct_answer: @WebMvcTest limits component scanning to MVC-related types and does not discover ordinary service or repository beans. It does include supported web infrastructure such as controllers, advice, converters, filters, and security configuration types. Supply a controller dependency with `@MockitoBean` (or older `@MockBean`) or import a small real configuration when that is what the test needs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what the slice actually excludes and how to handle missing dependencies in controller tests
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming every application bean is discovered by the MVC slice or that every missing collaborator must be mocked
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that filters and security auto-configuration may participate when Spring Security is present, and that the test should model authentication rather than disable security by habit

sections.title: What Gets Left Behind in @WebMvcTest
sections.content:
@WebMvcTest limits component scanning to supported MVC-related types; it does not perform ordinary application-wide discovery of service and repository beans. It may still include controllers, controller advice, JSON components, converters, filters, WebMvcConfigurer, security configuration types, imported configuration, and explicit test bean overrides.

When a controller needs a collaborator outside the slice, choose deliberately: use current **@MockitoBean** or older Boot **@MockBean** for a controlled mock, **@Import** a small real component, or define a test bean. Needing one real collaborator does not automatically require @SpringBootTest. Database infrastructure is normally outside this slice unless the test explicitly adds it.

sections.title: Loaded vs Excluded
sections.content:
emerald|Supported MVC types|~Slice candidates|controllers and advice|converters and filters|MockMvc infrastructure
rose|Not ordinarily discovered|~Outside slice scanning|service beans|repository beans|database infrastructure
amber|You can supply|~Match test intent|@MockitoBean current|@MockBean older Boot|@Import or test configuration

sections.title: Handling Missing Dependencies with @MockBean
When This Knowledge Matters
sections.content: This knowledge matters when the test context fails because a controller collaborator is absent, or when an unexpected filter changes the response. Mock a collaborator when only its contract matters; import a real one when its web-facing behavior belongs in the scenario; use broader integration only when the requirement crosses that boundary. With Spring Security present, security auto-configuration and filters may affect MockMvc requests, so authenticated scenarios can use Spring Security test support such as @WithMockUser. The exact status still depends on the configured entry point and access-denied handling.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating the slice as an exact bean whitelist**: Imports and supported web configuration types can add beans beyond the selected controller.
- **Using a fixed dependency-count rule**: The design problem is unclear responsibilities, not a universal maximum number.
- **Disabling security to make the test green**: If security is part of the public behavior, model an authenticated or unauthenticated request and assert the expected result.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Limited scanning**: Ordinary service and repository beans are not discovered by the MVC slice
**Supported web types**: Controllers, advice, converters, filters, WebMvcConfigurer, and security configuration types may participate
**Supply collaborators deliberately**: Use @MockitoBean, older @MockBean, @Import, or test configuration according to the boundary
**Security behavior is configuration-dependent**: Filters may protect MockMvc requests; method security is enforced only when it is enabled and proxied
**No fixed timing**: The slice normally loads less, but imports and configuration determine its actual startup cost

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @WebMvcTest limits discovery to MVC-related types, so ordinary service and repository beans are normally absent. It can still include controller advice, converters, filters, security configuration types, imports, and explicit test beans. If a controller collaborator is missing, I provide a Mockito bean override with @MockitoBean, use @MockBean on older Boot, or import a small real configuration when that behavior belongs in the test. With Spring Security present, filter-chain behavior may affect MockMvc requests, so I model the relevant user and authorization scenario instead of disabling security automatically.

questions.question: How do you test a POST endpoint with a request body using @WebMvcTest and MockMvc?
questions.title: Testing POST Endpoint with MockMvc
questions.direct_answer: For an endpoint that consumes JSON, perform the real POST route with `contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)` and a JSON body, then assert the status, headers, and response fields defined by that endpoint. `ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString(request)` keeps the body consistent with Java serialization. A creation endpoint commonly returns 201, but the API contract decides the expected status.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical MockMvc knowledge for POST requests—slightly harder than GET and very commonly asked in interviews
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting to set contentType(APPLICATION_JSON), which causes HTTP 415 Unsupported Media Type, or not knowing how to serialize the request body
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both manual JSON string construction and using ObjectMapper to serialize a Java object, and explain why content type is required

sections.title: Testing POST Endpoints with MockMvc
sections.content:
A POST test should reproduce the request contract. For an endpoint that consumes JSON, provide the real path, `Content-Type: application/json`, and a valid JSON body. `ObjectMapper.writeValueAsString(request)` is useful because it uses the same Java serialization rules as the application. Arrange only the collaborator behavior needed for the scenario.

Then assert the endpoint's actual response contract. A resource-creation endpoint often returns **201 Created**, may include a `Location` header, and may return the created representation, but none of those details is automatic for every POST. Validation failures, unsupported media types, authentication failures, and business conflicts should use the statuses and bodies defined by the API.

sections.title: POST Request Test Flow
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[perform POST /api/orders
JSON body] --> B[Controller
@RequestBody + @Valid] B --> C[@MockBean service
when..thenReturn] C --> D[201 Created] D --> E[andExpect status isCreated
+ jsonPath id] ```

sections.title: POST Request Test with ObjectMapper
When to Write This Test
sections.content:
Use a POST MVC test when you need evidence about request deserialization, validation, controller mapping, status, headers, response serialization, advice, filters, or security. For a create endpoint, check the success contract and representative failures such as malformed JSON, a missing required field, an unauthenticated request, or a conflict when the API defines those cases.

Keep service algorithms in focused tests when no MVC behavior is involved. Add broader integration coverage when the result depends on persistence, transactions, messaging, or another real boundary.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using the wrong media type**: A JSON-consuming mapping may return 415 when the request omits or changes `application/json`; assert the behavior defined by that mapping.
- **Writing fragile JSON by hand**: Use ObjectMapper for normal request objects, and write raw JSON only when malformed input is the test case.
- **Matching the exact pre-serialization object**: MVC creates a different request instance. Match meaningful arguments or capture and inspect them rather than depending on object identity.
- **Assuming every POST returns 201**: Creation commonly uses 201, while commands, searches, and asynchronous work can use other contracts. Assert the endpoint specification.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **Three required parts**: POST method via post(path), content type via contentType(APPLICATION_JSON), and JSON body via content(jsonString)
**ObjectMapper for serialization**: Inject @Autowired ObjectMapper and call writeValueAsString(object) to convert Java object to JSON safely
**Media type follows the mapping**: A JSON-consuming endpoint needs an application/json request; other POST endpoints may consume forms, multipart data, or another type
**Stub with any()**: Use when(service.createOrder(any(Order.class))) because MockMvc deserializes JSON into a new object instance
**Expected status follows the API**: Resource creation commonly returns 201, but POST does not imply one universal status

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: For a POST endpoint that consumes JSON, I select the controller with @WebMvcTest, inject MockMvc and ObjectMapper, and provide any missing collaborator. I serialize a request object with `writeValueAsString`, set `application/json`, and perform the real route. Then I assert the response defined by that endpoint—for a normal creation this may be 201, a Location header, and the generated id. MVC deserializes the body into a new object, so Mockito setup should match meaningful arguments rather than the original object's identity. I also cover invalid JSON and validation errors. This proves the MVC contract; persistence and transaction behavior need the appropriate broader test.

followup_questions: How do you test validation errors — for example, when a required field is missing?
How do you assert the response body's JSON structure with jsonPath?

questions.question: How do you test that a controller returns a 404 when a resource is not found?
questions.title: Testing 404 in @WebMvcTest
questions.direct_answer: Arrange the not-found path, call it with MockMvc, and assert `status().isNotFound()` plus the public error body. The application must map the condition to 404, but `@ControllerAdvice` is only one option; a controller may use `ResponseStatusException`, or an exception may carry `@ResponseStatus`. The test should exercise the mapping the application actually uses.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to test error paths and exception handling in Spring controllers—not just the happy path where everything succeeds
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing tests that only verify successful cases and forgetting to test edge cases like missing resources, which are critical for production-ready APIs
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that without @ControllerAdvice or @ExceptionHandler, the exception becomes a 500 Internal Server Error—showing you understand Spring's exception handling chain

sections.title: Testing 404 Responses in Spring Controllers
sections.content:
A 404 test verifies the API's contract for a missing single resource. Arrange the controller's not-found path—perhaps a service returns empty or throws a domain exception—perform the real request, and assert **404 Not Found** plus the stable public error body.

The not-found condition must be mapped to 404. An application can do that through `@ControllerAdvice`, `@ResponseStatus`, `ResponseStatusException`, or direct response handling. A plain custom RuntimeException does not automatically mean 404. The MVC test should include and exercise the mapping the application actually uses.

sections.title: How a 404 Is Produced and Asserted
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR A[GET /api/orders/99] --> B[Controller] B --> C[Service reports
missing order] C --> D[Controller throws or returns
a mapped not-found result] D --> E[Exception resolver or
direct response] E --> F[404 + public error body] F --> G[MockMvc assertions] ```

sections.title: Testing 404 with MockMvc and Exception Handling
When to Test 404 Responses
sections.content:
Use a 404 case for a missing resource addressed by a specific identifier when the API defines that result, such as `GET /api/products/{id}`. A collection search commonly returns `200 OK` with an empty array rather than 404, so follow the endpoint contract. A repeated DELETE may return 404, 204, or another documented result while still being idempotent.

Clients can use 404 for user feedback and negative caching according to HTTP rules. They should not normally retry it as if it were a temporary server failure. Assert the status and a safe, stable error representation without exposing a stack trace or internal database detail.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Assuming a custom exception automatically becomes 404**: Include the application's `@ControllerAdvice`, `@ResponseStatus`, `ResponseStatusException`, or direct mapping in the test boundary.
- **Returning 404 for every empty result**: A missing item and an empty collection are different API contracts.
- **Exposing exception details**: Check a stable public error body rather than a stack trace, SQL message, or internal class name.
- **Testing only success**: A not-found branch can have different advice, serialization, and security behavior and deserves its own MVC test.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **when().thenThrow()**: Mockito method that stubs a service call to throw an exception instead of returning a value—essential for testing error paths
**Exception mapping**: @ControllerAdvice is one option; @ResponseStatus, ResponseStatusException, or direct response handling can also define 404
**@ExceptionHandler**: Method-level annotation that maps specific exception types to HTTP responses—like catch blocks for controllers
**@ResponseStatus**: Annotation that sets the HTTP status code for an exception handler—NOT_FOUND maps to 404
**status().isNotFound()**: MockMvc assertion that verifies HTTP 404 response—equivalent to checking status code 404

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I arrange the application's missing-resource path, perform the request with MockMvc, and assert 404 plus the public error body. If the service throws `ResourceNotFoundException`, the MVC test must include the real mapping—perhaps `@ControllerAdvice`, an annotation on the exception, or another configured handler. A plain custom exception is not automatically a 404. I also keep the resource contract precise: a missing item may be 404, while an empty collection often remains 200 with `[]`. The test verifies status, content type, and safe client-facing fields without exposing internal exception details.

How would you test a 400 Bad Request from a validation failure?

questions.question: What is the difference between @WebMvcTest and @SpringBootTest for testing a controller?
questions.title: @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest for Controllers
questions.direct_answer: @WebMvcTest creates a focused MVC test slice and auto-configures MockMvc without starting a server. @SpringBootTest creates a broader Boot ApplicationContext and can start a server for RANDOM_PORT or DEFINED_PORT. Neither has a fixed startup time, and neither automatically proves every external integration; choose the smallest boundary that includes the behavior under test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the test boundary matches the MVC behavior or broader Boot wiring that the scenario needs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming @WebMvcTest has one fixed bean list or @SpringBootTest automatically supplies a real database, server, and every integration
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: State the exact mappings, filters, services, persistence, server, and external systems that are real or replaced in each test

sections.title: Choosing Between @WebMvcTest and @SpringBootTest
sections.content:
@WebMvcTest creates a focused Spring MVC slice and auto-configures MockMvc without opening a server port. It limits scanning to supported MVC-related types, so ordinary service and repository beans are normally absent. @SpringBootTest creates a broader Boot ApplicationContext through SpringApplication. Its profiles, properties, exclusions, mocks, and webEnvironment determine the beans and resources that actually start.

The decision is about **boundary**, not a fixed speed ratio. Use @WebMvcTest for mapping, validation, serialization, advice, filters, and security behavior at the MVC boundary. Use @SpringBootTest when the scenario needs broader Boot wiring. Neither annotation by itself guarantees a real database, every external connection, or production-identical behavior.

sections.title: @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest
sections.content:
blue|@WebMvcTest|~MVC slice|supported web types|MockMvc auto-configured|no listening server
violet|@SpringBootTest|~Broad Boot context|test-selected configuration|server only for port modes|external resources not guaranteed
emerald|Decision|~Choose the needed boundary|MVC contract -> slice|cross-layer Boot wiring -> broader test|measure cost

Boot context selected by the test configuration
Not discovered normally; can be added explicitly
Only if the test configures one
Provide missing collaborators with a mock or import
Beans present in the context can be injected
MVC contract and selected web behavior
Broader Boot wiring selected by the test

sections.title: Same Controller, Two Test Styles
When to Use Each Annotation
sections.content: Use **@WebMvcTest** when the requirement is the MVC contract: mappings, validation, status codes, response serialization, controller advice, filters, or security at that boundary. Use **@SpringBootTest** when the behavior genuinely needs broader Boot wiring, such as a controller working with real service and persistence components configured for the test. Choose from the behavior, not the class or method name. A controller test may need broad integration, while an endpoint contract can often be proved with a slice.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Choosing by habit**: Use the smallest boundary that contains the behavior, not one annotation for every controller test.
- **Leaving slice collaborators absent**: Provide them with @MockitoBean, older @MockBean, @Import, or test configuration.
- **Assuming a broad context means no mocks**: Selective bean overrides can be useful when one remote dependency is outside the test scope.
- **Calling a test end-to-end without real boundaries**: State which server, database, broker, or external system is actually present.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **@WebMvcTest**: MVC slice that limits scanning and auto-configuration to supported web concerns and test-selected additions
**@SpringBootTest**: Broad Boot context whose actual beans and resources depend on test configuration
**MockMvc**: Provided automatically by @WebMvcTest for making HTTP requests in tests—not available by default in @SpringBootTest unless you add @AutoConfigureMockMvc
**Missing collaborators**: Supply them with current @MockitoBean, older @MockBean, or a small real import
**Startup time**: The MVC slice usually has less setup, but there is no universal speed ratio

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @WebMvcTest creates a focused MVC slice and auto-configures MockMvc without a real server port. Ordinary services and repositories are outside its scanning, so I provide required collaborators with @MockitoBean, older @MockBean, or a small import. @SpringBootTest creates a broader Boot context, but the test's profiles, properties, mocks, exclusions, and webEnvironment still decide what starts. I choose @WebMvcTest for the MVC contract and @SpringBootTest when broader application wiring is part of the requirement. Neither has a fixed startup time, and @SpringBootTest does not automatically prove every database or external integration.

questions.question: How do you use jsonPath() in MockMvc to assert on the response body?
questions.title: Using jsonPath() in MockMvc
questions.direct_answer: `jsonPath()` applies a JsonPath expression to the response JSON and lets MockMvc assert the selected value. `$` is the document root, so `jsonPath("$.name").value("Asha")` checks one object field and `jsonPath("$[0].id").value(10)` checks the first array item. Pair content assertions with the expected status and content type.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical knowledge of selecting and asserting JSON response fields with MockMvc
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only checking HTTP status codes without verifying response content, or not understanding JsonPath syntax like dollar-dot for fields and dollar-bracket-zero for array elements
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show object, nested, and array paths, distinguish a null value from an absent field, and choose JsonPath or DTO deserialization according to the contract being checked

sections.title: Using jsonPath() to Assert on JSON Responses
sections.content:
**jsonPath()** is a MockMvc result matcher for selecting data from a JSON response and applying an assertion. A JsonPath expression begins at `$`, the document root. `$.userId` selects a root property, `$.address.city` selects a nested property, and `$[0].name` selects a property from the first array item.

Use `value(...)` for an expected value and matchers such as `exists()`, `doesNotExist()`, `isArray()`, or Hamcrest matchers when they express the contract. JsonPath is useful for a few selected fields. Deserializing into a DTO can be clearer when the whole response shape or Java mapping is the subject of the test; neither approach is universally better.

sections.content:
blue|Syntax|~JSONPath expressions|$ = root|$.field = property|$.list[0] = first item
emerald|Matchers|~assert values|value(x)|isArray() / hasSize(n)|exists() / doesNotExist()
amber|Why|~no deserialization|Assert the body directly|Readable contract checks

sections.title: jsonPath Assertions for Different JSON Structures
When to Use jsonPath Assertions
sections.content:
Use **jsonPath()** when a test needs to assert selected JSON fields without mapping the entire response. Examples include a created resource id, pagination metadata, a nested address, an array item, or a stable error field.

Pair body assertions with the expected status and content type. Avoid asserting every incidental field, array order, or internal message unless it is part of the public contract. When the complete response DTO and its deserialization matter, mapping the body to that type may provide clearer evidence.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Checking status only**: Assert the stable response data that makes the scenario meaningful.
- **Using the wrong root shape**: `$.id` selects an object property, while `$[0].id` starts from an array.
- **Confusing null with absence**: A present field whose value is null is different from a field that does not exist; choose the matching assertion.
- **Over-specifying the response**: Do not lock the test to incidental fields or array order that the API does not promise.
- **Rejecting DTO mapping by rule**: JsonPath suits selected fields; full deserialization can suit a complete typed contract.

sections.title: Quick revision
content: **jsonPath()**: MockMvc matcher for selecting JSON response data with a JsonPath expression
**$ (dollar sign)**: Represents the root of the JSON document in JsonPath expressions—all paths start with this symbol
**Dot notation**: $.field.nested accesses nested object properties—like navigating folders in a file system
**Bracket notation**: $[0] accesses array elements by index, starting from zero—similar to Java array access
**value() matcher**: Asserts that a JsonPath expression evaluates to a specific value—can compare strings, numbers, or booleans

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: `jsonPath()` selects part of a JSON response and applies a MockMvc assertion. `$` means the document root, so `$.name` checks a root property, `$.address.city` reaches a nested property, and `$[0].id` checks the first item in a root array. I pair those assertions with the expected status and content type. I use JsonPath when a few response fields define the scenario, and I can use `exists()`, `doesNotExist()`, array-size matchers, or `value(...)` as needed. If the complete typed response is important, deserializing it into a DTO can be clearer. The test should assert the public contract without depending on fields or ordering the API never promised.
